subject: History
title: Reform Movements and Muslim Revivalists
learningOutcomes: Describe the challenges faced by the Muslims after the decline of the Mughals.
Explain the contributions of Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani and Shah Waliullah to the revival of Islam.
Describe the Faraizi Movement of Haji Shariatullah and the Jihad Movement of Syed Ahmed Barelvi.
Explain the social, political and educational contributions of Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and the Aligarh Movement.
Identify the educational institutions of Deoband and Nadvat-ul-Ulema, and the Hindu revivalist movements of the same period.

sections.heading: Colonialism and the Revival of Islam
sections.body: After the decline of the Mughals, the British introduced new educational and social policies to create natives who were Indian by birth but European in outlook. In reaction, Muslim scholars began to revive Islamic teachings to improve the moral and social condition of the Muslims and to reclaim their former glory. These reformers were pioneers in creating a sense of national identity among the Muslims of the subcontinent.

sections.heading: Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani (Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi)
sections.body: Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi (born 1564, died 1624 CE), known as Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani ("reviver"), worked to purify Muslim beliefs. He opposed Emperor Akbar’s Deen-e-Illahi, organised the Naqshbandiya order, and wrote the book Tauheed-e-Shuhudi. Emperor Jehangir imprisoned him for two years for refusing to bow, then released him and reversed the un-Islamic laws of Akbar.

sections.heading: Shah Waliullah (1703–1762 CE)
sections.body: Shah Waliullah was educated in his father’s Madrasah-e-Rahimia. He translated the Holy Quran into Persian so that Muslims could understand it, wrote fifty-four books including Hujjat-ullah-al-Baligha, and tried to unite the Muslim sects. He said the Muslims declined because of social evils and luxuries, and invited Ahmed Shah Abdali to defeat the Marathas.

sections.heading: Haji Shariatullah and the Faraizi Movement
sections.body: Haji Shariatullah (1781–1840 CE), born in Faridpur, Bengal, started the peaceful Faraizi Movement in 1819. He urged Muslims to follow only the Faraiz (duties of Allah). It revived Muslim life in Bengal and protected the peasants. His son Mohsin-ud-Din (Dadu Miyan) continued it until the movement ended with his death in 1862.

sections.heading: Syed Ahmed Shaheed Barelvi and the Jihad Movement
sections.body: Syed Ahmed Shaheed Barelvi (1786–1831 CE) started the Jihad Movement to replace Sikh and British rule with Muslim rule. In 1826 he gathered an army of Mujahideen, captured Peshawar and set up a Muslim state under Shariah. He was pushed back to Kashmir by Ranjit Singh and was martyred at Balakot (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa).

sections.heading: Condition of Muslims after 1857 and Sir Syed Ahmed Khan
sections.body: The British blamed the Muslims for the 1857 War, so their condition became worse. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–1898 CE), born in Delhi, worked to reform the Muslims. He wrote the pamphlet "Causes of the Indian Revolt" and gave a three-point agenda: stay away from politics, bridge the gap with the British, and get educated for government jobs.

sections.heading: Educational Services of Sir Syed and the Aligarh Movement
sections.body: Sir Syed set up madrasahs in Muradabad and Ghaziabad, the Scientific Society (1864), and the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental School (1875), which became Aligarh College (1877) and later Aligarh University (chartered 1920). He inaugurated the Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886), wrote in Tehzib-ul-Ikhlaq, and proposed a separate electorate in 1883 — the basis of the Two Nation Theory.

sections.heading: Deoband, Nadvat-ul-Ulema and Hindu Revivalist Movements
sections.body: Darul-Uloom Deoband (1866), headed by Maulana Muhammad Qasim Nanotvi, taught the Dars-e-Nizami syllabus. Nadvat-ul-Ulema was established at Kanpur in 1892 and shifted to Lucknow in 1898. Among the Hindus, the Bhakti Movement (8th century) gave birth to Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak; and the Arya Samaj was founded in Bombay in 1875 by Dayananda Sarasvati.

definitions.definition: A "reviver" — one who revives the true teachings of Islam.
A religion introduced by Akbar that mixed Hindu and Muslim practices.
The duties or commandments of Allah, followed in the Faraizi Movement.
Muslim volunteers who struggle or fight for a religious cause.
The idea that the Muslims and Hindus of the subcontinent were two separate nations.
Sir Syed’s movement to spread modern education and remove Muslim misconceptions about the British.
The 17th-century Indo-Islamic syllabus used at Darul-Uloom Deoband.
A Hindu movement of devotion to God that gave birth to Sikhism.

examTips: Learn the key dates: Faraizi Movement 1819, MAO School 1875, Aligarh College 1877, Educational Conference 1886, Deoband 1866, Nadvat 1892.
Do not confuse the peaceful Faraizi Movement (Haji Shariatullah, Bengal) with the armed Jihad Movement (Syed Ahmed Barelvi, North-West).
Remember that Sir Syed’s separate electorate proposal (1883) became the basis of the Two Nation Theory.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore each Muslim reformer on the revival timeline. Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani
hotspots.fact: Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi (1564–1624) opposed Akbar’s Deen-e-Illahi and wrote Tauheed-e-Shuhudi.

hotspots.label: Shah Waliullah
hotspots.fact: Shah Waliullah (1703–1762) translated the Quran into Persian and wrote 54 books.

hotspots.label: Haji Shariatullah
hotspots.fact: Haji Shariatullah started the peaceful Faraizi Movement in Bengal in 1819.

hotspots.label: Syed Ahmed Barelvi
hotspots.fact: Syed Ahmed Barelvi (1786–1831) led the Jihad Movement and was martyred at Balakot.

hotspots.label: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan
hotspots.fact: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–1898) founded the Aligarh Movement and proposed the separate electorate.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange these Muslim reformers in order of their birth, earliest first.
sequencingActivity.explanation: By birth year: Ahmad Sirhindi (1564) → Shah Waliullah (1703) → Haji Shariatullah (1781) → Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why is Ahmad Sirhindi remembered as Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani ("reviver of Islam")?

options: He translated the Quran into Persian
He purified Muslim beliefs and opposed Akbar’s Deen-e-Illahi

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: He revived true Islamic teaching and opposed the mixed practices of Deen-e-Illahi.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: What best explains why the Faraizi Movement is called a peaceful reform movement?

options: It used an army of Mujahideen
It urged Muslims to follow their duties and protected peasants without violence

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: It reminded Muslims of the Faraiz and defended peasants peacefully, without armed conflict.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Although the Muslim state at Peshawar did not last, why is Syed Ahmed Barelvi’s Jihad Movement still important?

options: It raised Muslim morale and inspired later anti-British and freedom efforts

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: His struggle boosted Muslim morale and inspired later movements, even though the state was short-lived.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: How did the Aligarh Movement help pave the way for a separate Muslim homeland?

options: By spreading modern education and the spirit of Muslim Nationalism that led to the Two Nation Theory
By supporting the Indian National Congress

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Its students became pioneers of the Two Nation Theory, which led towards the creation of Pakistan.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why did Sir Syed advise Muslims to build good relations with the British instead of joining active politics?

options: He wanted Muslims to give up their identity
He believed education and better relations would first help Muslims recover from their weak post-1857 position

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: After 1857 the Muslims were weak and blamed for the revolt; Sir Syed felt education and trust must come first.
